Monday. Karthik had his guitar case by the door when Binita sighed down the phone. "Go, enjoy. I'll just sit here alone again." He put the guitar back. Band practice happened without him.
Thursday. He had skipped three practices in two weeks. Sitting in the college library, he made two lists. One: times he had actually let Binita down, like arriving an hour late to her exam-result dinner. He had apologised for that, and meant it. Two: times he felt guilty only because she sulked. The second list was much longer.
The following Monday. "I'm going to practice tonight," he told her. "I'll call you at nine." Binita went quiet, then said, "Fine, whatever you want." His stomach twisted, but he picked up the guitar. At nine he called, as promised. She was cool at first, then asked about the new song.

qa.q: How many practices had Karthik skipped in two weeks?
qa.a: Karthik had skipped three practices in two weeks.

qa.q: What did Karthik feel when Binita said "Fine, whatever you want"?
qa.a: He felt guilty and uneasy, his stomach twisting, because her coolness still pulled at him even though he had done nothing wrong.

qa.q: Why was Karthik's two-list exercise in the library a turning point?
qa.a: It helped him separate a real wrong, the late dinner that deserved an apology, from guilt that came only from sulking, so he could go to practice and still keep his promise to call.

qa.q: How might Binita experience Karthik going to practice and calling at nine?
qa.a: She may feel left out at first, which is why she went quiet, but the promised call showed he still cared, and she warmed up enough to ask about the new song.

grounding: A young man keeps giving up band practice when Binita sighs and sulks, then sorts real wrongs from pressure and goes while keeping in touch.

passage:
Wasim, you check your phone every time your mother calls, even mid-shift. Your Damini Aunty has nursed on this ward for thirty years. Listen to something from when I was twenty.
My Ammi raised four of us alone, and she never let me forget it. If I wanted to join the college trip, she would say, "Go. Who am I? Only the one who sold her bangles for your fees." Then she would not eat dinner. So I stayed. I missed the trip, the drama club, my best friend's wedding.
On the wedding day I was home, and Ammi was watching television, perfectly cheerful. I realised my staying had not made her happy. It had only stopped the sighing.
The next year I joined the drama club. I called her every evening at eight and let her sulk without fixing it. She sulked for a month. Then she came to my first play, in her best dupatta.

qa.q: What did Damini miss while she kept staying home?
qa.a: She missed the college trip, the drama club and her best friend's wedding.

qa.q: What did young Damini feel when she saw Ammi cheerful on the wedding day?
qa.a: She felt a jolt of clarity mixed with sadness, realising her staying had not made Ammi happy but had only stopped the sighing.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story changed things for young Damini?
qa.a: Joining the drama club while calling Ammi every evening at eight let her keep her own life and her care, without rushing to fix the sulking.

qa.q: How might Ammi have felt when she came to the first play?
qa.a: Ammi likely felt proud and a little relieved, and the best dupatta suggests the sulking had given way to respect for Damini's choice.

grounding: A senior nurse tells Wasim how, at twenty, she kept giving in to her mother's sighs and reminders of sacrifice until she chose her own plans while still calling home.

passage:
In the village near Hubli, Dilnaz had just told the family she'd been accepted for the nursing course in Bengaluru.
Her elder sister Yamini didn't say anything at first. She just sighed and went to the stove. Later, while they washed pots together, she said, "Of course you'll go. I left school at fifteen so you could study. But go."
Dilnaz's chest tightened. It was true. Yamini had worked in the fields for years, and Dilnaz had got the books. Every time she wanted something, the sighs came, and Dilnaz felt she owed her whole life.
That night she lay awake. Had she done Yamini wrong? Or was the guilt being used to keep her home?
Both, maybe. The sacrifice was real. Leaving wasn't a wrong.
In the morning she sat by Yamini. "Didi, I'll never forget what you gave up. I'm still going. And I want to help you finish school too, once I'm earning."

qa.q: Where is Dilnaz's nursing course?
qa.a: In Bengaluru.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz feeling as she lay awake?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt torn and guilty, unsure whether the guilt meant she had wronged Yamini or was being used to keep her home.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz decide, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She honoured Yamini's real sacrifice in words and with an offer of help, but kept her decision, since leaving for study was not a wrong.

qa.q: How might Yamini feel about Dilnaz leaving?
qa.a: Yamini may feel proud but also sad and a little resentful, remembering how much she gave up.

grounding: It shows a young adult caught by a sister's sighs and reminders of sacrifice, sorting real debt from guilt used as a lever.

passage:
Every Friday in Madrid, Pablo's friends met for tapas near the university, and every Friday, Clara went silent.
She never said no. She just sighed when he picked up his jacket. "Go. Have fun. I'll just stay here by myself again." Once she added, "I moved to this city for you."
So for a month, Pablo stayed. He told his friends he was tired. He watched films with Clara and felt her mood lift and his own sink.
One evening his friend Mateo called. "We miss you, man. Is everything okay?"
Pablo realised he'd stopped asking himself a simple question: had he done anything wrong by going out once a week? He hadn't. Clara's loneliness was real. But it wasn't his job to fix it by vanishing.
The next Friday he said, "I'll be back by eleven. Want to invite your colleague over while I'm out?" Clara sighed. He went anyway, and felt guilty for the first hour.

qa.q: Where did Pablo's friends meet every Friday?
qa.a: For tapas near the university.

qa.q: How did Pablo feel during the month he stayed home?
qa.a: Pablo felt guilty and low, his own mood sinking as he felt responsible for Clara's, giving in to avoid her sighs.

qa.q: What choice did Pablo make, and why?
qa.a: He asked whether going out once a week was actually wrong, decided it wasn't, and went, while suggesting Clara invite a colleague over.

qa.q: How might Clara see Pablo going out?
qa.a: Clara may feel lonely and hurt, since she moved cities for him, and sighs because she wants him to stay.

grounding: It shows a young adult giving in to a partner's sighs and reminders of sacrifice until he sees the guilt as a lever rather than a sign of harm.

passage: In the electronics lab, Afreen had just packed her bag when Ojas slumped against the bench. "So you're leaving. Cool. I'll just stay till midnight alone, like always." Afreen froze. This was the third evening this week. On Monday she had written his half of the report; on Wednesday she had skipped her sister's call to solder his board. Each time she said no, he sighed, went silent, and brought up how he'd lent her notes in first year. Her chest tightened now the same way. She asked herself a question she'd heard from the hostel counsellor: had she actually done something wrong? She hadn't. The circuit was his task, and she had finished hers. "I'm going, Ojas," she said, voice shaky. "I can look at your board with you tomorrow at ten, for an hour." He rolled his eyes. She walked out anyway, heart pounding, and then lighter.

qa.q: What had Afreen done for Ojas on Monday?
qa.a: On Monday she had written his half of the report.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling when Ojas slumped against the bench?
qa.a: Afreen felt a familiar guilt, her chest tightening, as if his mood were her responsibility to fix.

qa.q: What question helped Afreen, and why?
qa.a: Asking whether she had actually done something wrong showed her the guilt was working as a lever, since the circuit was Ojas's task and hers was finished.

qa.q: How might Ojas see Afreen's offer of an hour tomorrow?
qa.a: Ojas seems annoyed, rolling his eyes because the old pressure no longer works; later he may see the hour as fair help.

grounding: Shows a young adult who keeps giving in to sighs, sulking and reminders of past favours, and begins to test whether the guilt is real.
